blocks.text: [II, 772] Having thus set out the opinions of others, we shall here also present our own and try to support it with suitable arguments. First, I side with those who hold that פרס peres is a species of eagle. Among them are the Greeks, Jerome, the Chaldeans, the Arabs and most of the more recent writers. In favour of this is the fact that among the Macedonians, who enriched from the spoils of the East not only their wealth but also their language, the eagle was called παραὸς [paraos], in manifest allusion to the Hebrew פרס peres. Hesychius: Παραός· ἀετὸς ὑπὸ Μακεδόνων· [Paraos; aetos hypo Makedonōn;] Paraos, the eagle among the Macedonians. Moreover, just as by universal agreement נשר denotes the true eagle, so it is very probable that the words immediately following in Moses, namely פרס and עזניה, designate other species of eagles known to the Jews. Nor is it safe to oppose so many interpreters who hold this view. Let it stand firm, then, that פרס is among the species of eagles. But now we must inquire into the species, which can be extracted from nothing else than the origin of the word, since apart from the bare name we have nothing whatever about it. And Aben Ezra rightly [col. 187] notes that the origin is to be taken from these words of Es. LVIII, 7: פרוס לרעב לחמך Break your bread for the hungry. By this note he meant to indicate that it is a kind of eagle so called from breaking. But to make the matter clearer, consider, reader, these words of Mich. III, 3., which it is surprising have not yet been cited in this discussion: ואת עצמותיהם פצחו ופרשו כאשר בסיר וכבשר בתוך קלחת, And they broke their bones and shattered them as in a pot, and as flesh in the midst of a cauldron. From this it is evident that the verb פרס (or פרש with Sin Semol, which is the same) is also used of the breaking of bones. From this, then, there is no one who would not conclude that פרס peres is the ossifrage, that is, that species of eagle which from breaking bones is called in the Roman tongue ossifraga or ossifragus [bone-breaker], and in Arabic either simply كاسر [kāsir], that is, breaker, or كاسر اعظام [kāsir aʿẓām] breaker of bones ^{(1)}. Thus Junius rightly rendered it ossifrage, although the true reason for this rendering escaped him. And perhaps it bears on the same point that for פרס Onkelos and the Jerusalem Targum have ער or עריא. For the words ער and עריא, with the radicals inverted, could have been derived from the verbs רעע or רעה, which mean to break and to crush. Of the ossifrage Lucretius writes thus, book 5, line 1077:
Lastly the race of winged things, and the various birds, hawks and ossifrages — — —
